extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, language, and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory notes and critical commentaries on terminology, definition, categories, and propositions in formal and philosophical logic, aimed at clarifying correct usage and pitfalls in reasoning and definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify quoted references before trusting accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author is accused, with volume and page referred to, and the apparent guarantee of inverted commas, readers should not give implicit credence to the assertion without verifying the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning about perverse misquotation: verify references rather than assuming quotation marks and citation suffice to prove an accusation of dishonesty or inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using highly ambiguous general terms without hedging
rubrics_metrics.description: A term like 'Stone' is 'wholly unfit for accurate reasoning, unless hedged round on every occasion by other phrases; as building stone, precious stone, gall-stone, etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a name applies to widely different things with no single uniformly present quality, it should be restricted or qualified in context; otherwise methods of definition fail because of insufficient common ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise technical terminology to express relation between name and attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a term 'exclusively appropriated to express the manner in which a concrete general name serves to mark the attributes which are involved in its signification' (i.e., a precise technical word for connotation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because common words like 'involve' or 'imply' are too general, a narrowly defined technical term (as the schoolmen used 'to connote') helps avoid confusion in philosophy of language and logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation (technical): connoted are forms/attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: In the technical sense used by the schoolmen, 'nothing was said to be connoted except forms,' which can be understood as synonymous with 'attributes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using 'to connote' in technical logical discussion, restrict it to the marking of attributes (forms) rather than broader etymological senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denotation determined by predicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of what a name denotes is what it can be predicated of: we can predicate of a sound or a smell that it is not white; affirmation and negation divide the whole field of predication between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding denotation/extension of a term, check the class of objects of which the predicate can be asserted; this governs whether negative names name the complementary class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascription of attributes implies a percipient mind
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascribe any attribute to an object necessarily implies a mind to perceive it; objects are considered in relation to percipient minds when attributing properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing propositions about attributes, bear in mind the implicit role of a perceiver in the very act of predication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Categories as analyses of predicates rather than enumerations of namable things
rubrics_metrics.description: The Categories were intended as 'a generalization of predicates; an analysis of the final import of predication,' not as an enumeration of all kinds of things capable of being predicated of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'Under what Categories can we predicate regarding X?' rather than 'In what Category is X?'; Categories summarize the possible answers to predicate-questions (Quid sit? Quantum sit? Quale sit?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Feeling among Categories where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaint that the Categories had 'no Category of Feeling' even though feeling is predicable as a summum genus of particular feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classificatory schemes should account for the predicability of feelings and not omit feeling as a major logical category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must account for attributes of unique as well as class objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain's definition of attributes as 'points of community among classes' is limited because 'an object, unique in its kind, may be said to have attributes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid definitions that only apply to attributes shared by classes; allow for attributes of singular/unique objects and further analysis of those 'points of community.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear nomenclature reflecting logical function (Total/Partial vs Universal/Particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Bain proposes using 'Total' and 'Partial' for propositions (reserving 'Universal' and 'Particular' for inductive meaning), arguing that Singular propositions align with Universal in syllogistic rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose terms whose senses align with the role they play in reasoning; be aware of the double meanings of terms and the benefits/tradeoffs of renaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish knowledge-required actions from instinctive actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Human use of tools (e.g., using a spade) requires knowledge of the tool and of the earth; contrast with instincts (e.g., a mole digging) where uncertain what passes in the animal's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing intentional or cognitive states in examples, ensure the distinction between learned/reflective actions and instinctive behaviors is respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: For logical purposes treat classes as indefinite rather than definite
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory in the text tacitly supposes all classes to be indefinite; for Logic 'definite classes, as such, are almost useless; though often serviceable as means of abridged expression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In formal logical analysis, prefer indefinite (unenumerated) class-conceptions (e.g., 'men,' 'poets') rather than enumerated definite classes (e.g., 'the Peers of the Realm').

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize tacit errors of sense and cogitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tacit errors are made by passing from one imagination to another different thing; by feigning that to be past or future which never was nor shall be; by mistaking signs for what they signify, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing reasoning or perception, look for these common sources of error (misapplied imagination, misreading signs, false inference from custom) as distinct error types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat propositions asserting mere Existence as elliptical and resolvable
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions that predicate mere existence are 'more or less abbreviated, or elliptical' and when fully expressed fall under co-existence or succession (causation); e.g., 'Are we to say that a mole cannot dig except he has an idea of the ground?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating 'existence' as a primitive predicate; rephrase questions of existence into more precise causal or co-existent relational propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about using 'Being' as a summum genus in classificatory schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Bain thinks the classification of Nature up to one summum genus, Being or that which Exists, is 'fictitious and unmeaning' because perception is always by contrast and we have no other class to oppose to Being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not elevate 'Being' (existence) as a highest logical genus without recognizing its potential vacuity or lack of contrast class in logical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between verbal (analytic) and real (informative) propositions in defining terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition that affirms an attribute already signified by a name adds no information (verbal); a real proposition conveys information about facts not implicit in common usage of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing definitions and propositions, determine whether a statement is merely tautological given the ordinary meaning of words, or conveys new factual content; common/specialist connotation matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions should reflect ordinary/general connotation unless explicitly scientific
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of a word (special scientific connotation apart) connotes only the properties which it is a mark of in the general mind; therefore new scientific discoveries should not be folded into the ordinary meaning of a common term without special notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat specialized, learned properties as part of a term's common meaning for purposes of everyday logical arguments; clearly mark when a technical or scientific connotation is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real Definition vs Nominal Definition: purposes differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Archbishop Whately limits 'Real Definition' to one which 'explains any thing more of the nature of the thing than is implied in the name'; De Morgan reverses this and allows a real definition to be any explanation sufficient to separate the things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether a definition aims to convey additional knowledge of nature (real definition) or simply to supply a distinguishing rule (sufficient-for-distinction definition) and choose formulation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate definitional content from factual premises in syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: In syllogistic examples involving imaginary creatures, the definition (e.g., what a dragon is) differs from a factual assertion; a false minor premise may be a false statement of fact but not a false definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating syllogistic validity, separate what is contained in the definition of a term from empirical claims about instances; invalid conclusions may arise from conflating the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of equivalent propositional forms (equipollency/obversion/conversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different cases of Equipollency, or 'Equivalent Propositional Forms,' such as obversion (changing an affirmation to denying its negative), are common and set forth in logical works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognized transformations (obversion, conversion, etc.) correctly when converting or testing propositions for equivalence; be mindful of forms that preserve truth and those that do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care in classifying Singular propositions within syllogistic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Bain denies the claim of Singular Propositions to be classed, for ratiocination, with Universal, though they follow the same rules as Universal; he would exclude them from the syllogism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying syllogistic rules, explicitly decide how to handle singular propositions (e.g., 'Socrates is wise') — whether to treat them as Total/Universal analogues or as special cases requiring separate handling.
